slot.brief: Why does H2O have abnormally high boiling point compared to H2S — explain via intermolecular hydrogen bonding (statement/one-liner).

stem: Why does water have a much higher boiling point than hydrogen sulfide?
options: Water molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds; hydrogen sulfide does not form comparable bonds.
Water has a lower molar mass, so its molecules move more slowly.
Hydrogen sulfide forms stronger intermolecular hydrogen bonds than water.
Water is non-polar, whereas hydrogen sulfide is polar.

verdicts.working: Water molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which require more energy to overcome than the intermolecular forces in H₂S. Thus (A) is correct.

working:
Intermolecular hydrogen bonding is strong in $\text{H}_2\text{O}$; it is not significant in $\text{H}_2\text{S}$. More energy is needed to separate water molecules.

Independent check: Water molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, which require more energy to overcome than the intermolecular forces in H₂S. Thus (A) is correct.
solution: Water molecules form strong intermolecular hydrogen bonds, whereas hydrogen sulfide does not form comparable bonds. Hence, more energy is required to separate water molecules, giving water a higher boiling point.
